newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil to boost credit for exporters, cut deficit.
newsitem.headline: Brazil to boost credit for exporters, cut deficit.

text.p: Brazil plans to give exporters new, improved credit terms in a bid to narrow the country's trade gap, but the changes do not mean a deficit disaster is looming, officials said.

The National Development Bank (BNDES) plans to cut interest charged on its 1.0 billion real credit line for exporters of manufactured goods, now about 20 percent per annum, and raise a limit of the value of each loan, a bank spokeswoman said.
The BNDES' Finamex credit line for capital goods exports may also be lengthened to 12 years from a current eight, she said.
Both credit lines offer loans equivalent to 85 percent of the value of exports.

Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros, the Finance Ministry's economic policy secretary, said that as well as changing export credit terms the BNDES was preparing new, low-interest credit lines for fruit, furniture and autoparts exporters.
"The trade balance results do not worry the government," Mendonca de Barros told reporters. "We are on the right path."
The new export credit programs come amid mounting concern that Brazil's trade deficit may be about to balloon.
Government officials have strenuously denied a report that October's deficit may be as high as $1.5 billion, forecasting instead a shortfall of about $500 million.
In 1996 as a whole, the deficit is likely to be close to last year's $3.157 billion gap, Central Bank director Chico Lopes said in a newspaper interview published Wednesday.

Mendonca de Barros said the export credit moves would bolster a new law exempting exports from the so-called ICMS tax on sales and circulation of goods and services, but the positive impact of the measures would take a few months to be felt.
"What really counts is the performance of the trade balance over the long term," Mendonca de Barros said.
Government officials also expect the ongoing privatization of Brazil's ports will boost exports next year.
"A trade deficit over two or three months isn't going to alter our policies," Planning Minister Antonio Kandir was quoted as saying by newspaper Gazeta Mercantil.
"We're in a comfortable position to wait for the results of ports privatization, the ICMS (bill) and reducing the cost of doing business in Brazil," he said.
